_comment: BENCHMARK INPUTS, SNAPSHOTTED BY IDENTITY AND NOT BY COPY.
sources/scope.md, 'Snapshots are append-only': each release archives the register state and
every fetched source version under a dated path with a SHA-256 manifest, and a prior entry is
never overwritten. The two benchmark inputs are held to that rule with one difference, and the
difference is a licence rather than a preference: THE BYTES ARE NOT ARCHIVED. The content of
both files is the IEA's Hydrogen Projects Database — directly in one case, quality-checked by
Odenweller and Ueckerdt in the other — and this repository is not licensed to redistribute it.
SO WHAT IS ARCHIVED IS THE IDENTITY: the publisher's URL, the day it was fetched, the size and
the SHA-256. That is enough for anybody to fetch the same file from the publisher and prove it
is the one these numbers were computed from, which is the whole purpose the snapshot rule
serves — 'the archive is what makes every published number reconstructible after the register
has moved on'. A hash does that without holding a copy nobody may pass on.
APPEND-ONLY, LIKE THE SNAPSHOTS. A refreshed benchmark is a NEW entry with a new date and a new
hash; the old one stays, because the counts in sources/hydrogen_docket.md and in pull request
#52 were computed against it and a reader checking them a year from now needs to know which
file they are about. sources/report_benchmark_gap.py verifies the live cache against the newest
entry per benchmark and says so on every run.
ONE BENCHMARK IN TWO VINTAGES, NOT TWO BENCHMARKS. Recorded 11 September 2026, after the
admission search made the relationship impossible to keep ignoring. Odenweller & Ueckerdt
(2025) IS the IEA's October 2023 database, quality-checked, and it keeps the IEA's own
reference numbers: 35 of the 54 references the search settled exist in both files under the
same number, 29 of them under the same name. The register had been treating them as two
independent lists and reaching for a NAME STEM to join rows that shared an identifier all
along — which is how a machine guess got into a class as a verdict (D54).
WHAT FOLLOWS FROM THE DEPENDENCY. The two files cannot be summed, cannot corroborate each
other, and a gap in one is not independent evidence of a gap in the other. What the older
vintage CAN do, and what it is now read for, is DRIFT: which entries left the list between
October 2023 and now, which were renamed, which are new. A project that vanishes from a
database is a project whose failure nobody counts (rule 17), and drift is the only place
that fact can be seen.

vintages.note: The live endpoint. The current vintage and the one the register measures against.

The IEA's October 2023 database, quality-checked, under the IEA's own reference numbering. NOT AN INDEPENDENT BENCHMARK: it cannot corroborate the live file because it is the live file's own past. It is read for drift between the two vintages and for nothing else.
